Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\left\lfloor \sqrt n\right\rfloor .
\]

Then

\[
m^2\le n\le (m+1)^2-1=m^2+2m.
\]

We will determine strong restrictions on the prime factors of \(n\).

---

### 1. Prime factor restrictions

Let \(p\mid n\) be a prime.

#### Case 1: \(p\le m\)

Then \(p\mid m!\), so

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 0 \pmod p.
\]

Since \(n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450\), we must have

\[
450\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

Thus any prime divisor of \(n\) that is at most \(m\) must be one of \(2,3,5\).

Moreover, if \(p\in\{2,3,5\}\) and \(p^a\parallel n\), then \(p^a\mid (m!)^{n!}\). Indeed, since \(p\mid m!\),

\[
(m!)^{n!}
\]

is divisible by \(p^{n!}\). Also \(p^a\mid n\) implies \(a\le n\le n!\), so \(p^a\mid (m!)^{n!}\). Therefore the divisibility condition forces

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

Hence the \(2,3,5\)-part of \(n\) divides \(450\).

#### Case 2: \(p>m\)

Then \(p\nmid m!\). Also \(p\mid n\), so \(p\le n\), which implies \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
451\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

so

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Therefore any prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, any prime \(p>m\) occurs to the first power in \(n\), because

\[
p^2\ge (m+1)^2>m^2+2m\ge n.
\]

---

### 2. Ruling out \(n>1230\)

Assume \(n>1230\). Since

\[
34^2+2\cdot 34=1224<1230,
\]

we must have \(m\ge 35\).

If \(m\ge 41\), then neither \(11\) nor \(41\) can divide \(n\), because those primes are not larger than \(m\). The only possible prime divisors are \(2,3,5\), and their full contribution divides \(450\). Hence \(n\mid 450\), so \(n\le 450\), contradiction.

Thus for \(n>1230\), we must have

\[
35\le m\le 40.
\]

In this range, \(11\le m\), so \(11\nmid n\). Since \(41>m\), the only possible prime beyond \(2,3,5\) is \(41\), and it appears at most once.

Therefore

\[
n=d \quad\text{or}\quad n=41d,
\]

where \(d\mid 450\).

If \(n=d\), then \(n\le 450<1230\), impossible.

If \(n=41d\), then since \(m\le 40\),

\[
n\le 40^2+2\cdot 40=1680,
\]

so

\[
d\le \frac{1680}{41}<41.
\]

The largest divisor of \(450\) not exceeding \(40\) is \(30\). Therefore

\[
n=41d\le 41\cdot 30=1230,
\]

contradicting \(n>1230\).

So no \(n>1230\) works.

---

### 3. Checking \(n=1230\)

We have

\[
\left\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\right\rfloor =35
\]

because

\[
35^2=1225<1230<1296=36^2.
\]

Also

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

For \(p=2,3,5\), since \(p\mid 35!\),

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 0\pmod p,
\]

and \(450\equiv 0\pmod p\). Thus these primes divide the expression.

For \(p=41\), since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat’s little theorem gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(2,3,5,41\) are pairwise coprime, their product \(1230\) divides

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Thus \(1230\) works, and no larger integer works.

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
